implementation_notes: C# 9 records give non-destructive mutation as syntax: `person with { Home = person.Home with { City = "Berlin" } }` returns a copy with the named members replaced, using the compiler-generated copy constructor and init-only setters, which replaces the hand-written setter cascade for one level and nests for depth. Immutable collections complete the picture with setters that return new collections instead of mutating (`ImmutableDictionary.SetItem`, `ImmutableList<T>.SetItem`). Hand-write a `Lens<T, U>` record (a getter plus a setter delegate) only when one focus must be stored, passed or reused across many update sites - the `with` expression is then still the implementation inside the setter.
pitfalls: `with` is a shallow copy: reference-type members (List<T>, arrays, class components) are shared with the original, so mutating one is visible through the other.
A record's value equality still uses reference equality for those nested reference members, so two records that look equal after an update can compare unequal.
`with` on a mutable struct copies the whole struct, and driving it through an interface (for example `IWith`/boxing) hides an extra copy per update.
